question: According to Eurostat, organic cereal production in the EU is less than 1% of non-organic yields in some categories. It will take many years to close this gap in organic farming, as the lag is very significant. Unfortunately, this lag cannot be solved without subsidies or government intervention, because organic farming is simply too small in comparison with conventional farming.

The low share of organic farming also indicates that organic farming is not financially viable or able to sustain itself. In addition, conventional farming uses large amounts of pesticides, which are highly damaging to human health, natural ecosystems and animal, pollinator and plant populations.
Therefore, in order to protect human health and prevent the destruction of nature and biodiversity, organic farming must grow. 1.
Does the Commission agree that the development of organic farming is an important factor in protecting human health and the environment?
What measures will the Commission take to significantly increase the scale of organic farming?
answer: 1. The Commission is fully aware of all the benefits (for water, air, soil, climate, environment, biodiversity, animal welfare, etc.) that organic farming has. Organic farming is a key avenue for the transition towards more sustainable agriculture and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) promotes and supports organic farming.

This is why the share of EU agricultural land receiving support for organic farming doubled compared to the previous CAP (2014-2020) from about 5% to about 10%. 2. Under the umbrella of the European Green Deal, both the Farm to Fork strategy (1) and the Biodiversity strategy (2) include the target of 25% of EU agricultural land under organic farming by 2030.

In support of the achievement of this target, the Commission has adopted on 25 March 2021 the EU Action Plan for the Development of Organic Production (COM(2021) 141), which it is currently implementing. This Action Plan aims to develop the demand for and supply of organic products, and to enhance further the sustainability of organic farming.

All the Member States offer financial support both for conversion and maintenance of organic farming in their CAP Strategic Plans for 2023-2027. The design of support for organic interventions varies: some Member States promote conversion and maintenance through eco-schemes in the first pillar, whereas some others offer this through rural development interventions.

Organic farmers can also benefit from support from other interventions such as knowledge transfer and innovation actions, advisory services, quality schemes for agricultural products and foodstuff (including promotion and information measures), investments, animal welfare and cooperation.
